clue.text: Two sections at rear of traffic problem

parts.note: the tail is the hindmost section of a creature or vehicle
the back is the rear section of anything

explanation.surface: A traffic jam described by the two lanes at the back of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The one phrase does double duty, each half of the answer being a word for the rear end of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A queue of stationary vehicles stretching back from an obstruction is a classic road-traffic problem.

clue.text: Charge-sheet, when artist gets caught up in quarrel

indicators.note: gets caught means is trapped inside, so the quarrel encloses the artist

parts.note: a tiff is a minor quarrel

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the artist is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: An artist gets dragged into a row and is handed a charge sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge-sheet' is not a police document but a list of charges, that is prices.
explanation.definitionFit: A tariff is a schedule of prices or duties, a sheet of charges.

clue.text: Spike with the demon drink

parts.note: an imp is a little demon
ale is beer, a drink

explanation.surface: Lacing the demon drink, so spiking it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spike' looks like adding alcohol to a drink, but it means to pierce.
explanation.definitionFit: To run something through with a sharp point is to impale it.

clue.text: Support for, say, cuckoo flower

definitions.meaning: what a bird such as a cuckoo stands on
a plant name, as in ... trefoil

explanation.surface: Something holding up a cuckooflower, a wild plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The cuckooflower is a real meadow plant, which hides the split after 'cuckoo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird stands on its foot; bird's-foot is also the name of a small leguminous plant.

clue.text: Lord's seat reflected his changing position

indicators.note: changing position says the letters of the two words move into new places

explanation.surface: A peer's opinion shifted as he moved around in his seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing position' signals the anagram of both words together. The deep sofa is named after an Earl of Chesterfield, hence a lord's seat.
explanation.definitionFit: The deep buttoned leather sofa bears the name of an Earl, so it is literally a lord's seat.

clue.text: Black sheepdog returned one having strayed to this pen

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: returned asks for the dog's letters to be read from the end back to the start
having strayed says the numeral one has wandered off and is no longer in the dog's letters

parts.note: a collie is the classic herding sheepdog
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A black sheepdog comes home short of one sheep, which has strayed into this pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having strayed' drops the I, and 'returned' turns what is left round after B. 'Pen' is not an enclosure for sheep but a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc was an Anglo-French author, and a pen is a common figure for a writer.

clue.text: Hard drug's wrapped up in old garment

indicators.note: wrapped means folded round, so the drug encloses the letter
up in a down clue means the drug is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: dope is a drug
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Hard drugs smuggled inside an ancient robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns DOPE into EPOD, and 'wrapped' puts H inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ephod was a sleeveless vestment worn by Jewish priests in biblical times.

clue.text: Belgian subject?

parts.note: a person from a Belgian city, read as a vassal owing feudal loyalty

explanation.definitionFit: A feudal vassal is a sworn subject; split, the word suggests a man from a city in Belgium.

clue.text: Light baskets with plants, including thyme, say

indicators.note: including means taking in, so the plants enclose the letter

parts.note: cresses are salad plants
thyme sounds like time, abbreviated T

explanation.surface: Baskets of herbs: cress, with some thyme for example.
explanation.walkthrough: Thyme stands for its sound-alike, time, whose abbreviation is T. 'Light' means lamp, not lightweight.
explanation.definitionFit: Cressets were iron baskets holding burning fuel, used as beacons or torches.

clue.text: Take on stout fellow for daily duties

parts.note: re means on, in the sense of concerning
porter is a dark beer much like stout

explanation.surface: Hiring a sturdy man to do the household chores every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' just tells you to put the pieces together. 'Stout' looks like a description of the man but is the drink, and 'daily' is a newspaper, not a cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist on a daily newspaper does the duty of gathering news for it.

clue.text: Breathe with difficulty in a gag

definitions.meaning: to breathe with a whistling, laboured sound, as with asthma
a joke or clever trick, an old-fashioned word for a scheme or jest

explanation.surface: Someone gasping for breath because they have been gagged.
explanation.definitionFit: Laboured, whistling breathing is the verb; a bright idea or jest is the noun sense.

clue.text: A goal for the opposition?

parts.note: an own goal read as an aim held by those working against each other

explanation.definitionFit: People at odds have opposing aims; a misunderstanding about intent is a muddle of aims.

clue.text: Uplands, i.e. downs

definitions.meaning: high moorland hills, as in the Lake District of northern England
knocks down, as when chopping a tree or flooring a boxer

explanation.surface: A geography joke: uplands are, oddly, the same as downs.
explanation.definitionFit: Northern English moorland hills share a spelling with the verb for felling, knocking to the ground.

clue.text: Lack of drive troubled residents.

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the word residents is stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Locals who are worried have lost their get-up-and-go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troubled' rearranges RESIDENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatigue means a lack of energy or drive.

clue.text: Exotic resorts feature in this maritime area

indicators.note: exotic means foreign or strange, so the word resorts takes on an unfamiliar arrangement

parts.note: a trait is a distinguishing feature

explanation.surface: Holiday resorts in faraway places are a feature of this stretch of sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exotic' signals the anagram of the seven letters. The Torres Strait lies between Australia and New Guinea.
explanation.definitionFit: The strait is a sea passage, a maritime region between Cape York and New Guinea.

clue.text: Town to consider 'carefully extended high-rise area

parts.note: NB, nota bene, means note well, consider carefully
a ridge is a long stretch of raised land

explanation.surface: A town planning to examine an extended tower-block estate.
explanation.walkthrough: TONBRIDGE is a town in Kent. 'High-rise' suggests flats, but it is raised ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonbridge is a market town in Kent, in south-east England.

clue.text: The European, Sun and Standard

parts.note: a Pole is a European from Poland
the sun is a star

explanation.surface: A list of newspapers: The European, the Sun and the Standard.
explanation.walkthrough: The European, the Sun and the (Evening) Standard were all British newspapers, a misleading surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The guiding star is a figurative principle to steer by, a standard.

clue.text: Clocking out

definitions.meaning: hitting, as in clocking someone on the jaw
on strike, as workers who walk out

explanation.surface: A worker punching the time clock at the end of a shift.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitting someone is clocking them; workers out on strike are taking industrial action.

clue.text: Undressing in public, leaving behind revealed?

parts.note: something out is revealed, made public
stripping is taking one's clothes off

explanation.surface: A streaker strips off in public, showing everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In public' just reinforces the picture of OUT: undressing that is out in the open.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstrip rivals is to go faster than them and leave them behind.

clue.text: About to curl up — getting shy?

parts.note: re means about, concerning
to coil is to curl up into rings

explanation.surface: Someone about to curl up because they are getting shy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' is the verb, to start back in fright as a horse does, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To flinch or draw back suddenly is to shy, as a startled horse does.

clue.text: Written article extracted from page nine

indicators.note: extracted from means pulled out of, so the article is removed from the group of nine

parts.note: an ennead is a group of nine
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A written piece taken from page nine of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extracted from' removes the article from the group of nine; 'page' looks like part of the newspaper picture but just supplies its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something penned has been written, as with a pen.

clue.text: 4, for example, always carrying gun

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always
a pistol is a hand gun

explanation.surface: An armed man who never goes anywhere without his gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to 4 down, the Earl of Chesterfield, famous for his letters to his son.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Chesterfield is best known for his published letters, so he is an example of a letter writer.

clue.text: This half-cut fool turned up drunk

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards
half-cut says only half of the word is kept, its first two letters

parts.note: a git is a fool, British slang

explanation.surface: A half-drunk idiot shows up plastered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is also British slang for drunk, but here keeps TH; TH + GIT read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is informal for intoxicated, tipsy.

clue.text: In here, everyone is doing bird

indicators.note: in says the bird is lying inside the words that follow, across the comma

explanation.surface: Everyone in this place is serving a prison sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing bird' is British slang for serving time in prison, a false scent for the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The female of the ruff, a wading bird, has its own name in ornithology.

clue.text: Pair with, for instance, back pain

parts.note: to twin is to pair one thing with another

indicators.note: back says the abbreviation is read from its end to its start

explanation.surface: Twinning with someone gives you, for example, back ache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like the site of the pain, but it is the reversal signal on the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden sharp stab of pain is a twinge.

clue.text: Be competent enough to retain control

definitions.meaning: keep a job by doing it adequately, as in managing to keep one's job
restrain, keep under, as in holding prices

explanation.surface: Being good enough at the job to keep charge of things.
explanation.definitionFit: One holds down a job by being competent at it; to hold down prices is to keep them in check.

clue.text: True love's verbal agreement

parts.note: right means true, correct
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A real lover's spoken promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as O comes from tennis scoring, where love means nil.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial word is a spoken expression of assent, an informal okay.

clue.text: Rose flower partly choked by long grass

indicators.note: choked by means smothered inside, so the grass surrounds the bloom

parts.note: a reed is a tall waterside grass
bell is part of many flower names, as in bluebell and harebell

explanation.surface: A rose being strangled by tall grasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the flower but is the past tense of rise, as in rising up against authority.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise up against rulers is to revolt; the past tense fits the clue's past form.
